name: desalination_scheduling
description: A seawater desalination plant with three parallel treatment trains, scheduled against a time-of-use tariff. An intake pump feeds a header that splits across three pretreatment units; each pretreatment unit feeds its own reverse-osmosis skid, whose permeate recombines into a shared post-treatment step and a product water pump. Brine leaves each RO skid to the ocean outfall. The plant owes a fixed volume of product water per month rather than an hour-by-hour profile, so the only question is when to make it: the comparison is a flat 24/7 baseline against a schedule that turns RO trains down and off through the tariff peak.

time._comment: A full calendar month at 15-minute resolution: 2976 time points. One calendar month is the longest horizon a single TimeBlock accepts (its max_length). The step is 15 minutes rather than an hour because the RO recuperation delay is 45 minutes and has to land on a whole number of steps; 15 min also divides the tariff's 16:00 and 21:00 boundaries exactly. The monthly water obligation is prorated onto this horizon (see demand), so a shorter horizon may be substituted without touching the demand figure.

demand._comment: 265 acre-feet of product water per month, measured downstream of the product water pump. There is no hourly profile: the plant owes a volume over the month and may place it anywhere in the horizon, which is exactly the flexibility this example prices. Prorated onto the horizon as volume_af_per_month * (horizon hours / hours in the calendar month the horizon starts in).

intake_pump._comment: Seawater intake pump: lifts and screens raw feed into the pretreatment header, on a feed basis. always_on attaches a status binary pinned at 1 for every step (see logic.always_on_min_flow_m3_per_hr for why its lower bound is zero rather than a turndown floor).

pretreatment._comment: One constant-energy-intensity unit per train, on the feed stream. always_on as for the intake pump: the status binary exists and is pinned at 1, so pretreatment never contributes a shutdown decision.

reverse_osmosis._comment: One RO skid per train, fed by that train's pretreatment unit. energy_intensity_basis says which stream the intensity is quoted against: 'permeate' (3.31 kWh per m3 of product, the commonly quoted specific energy, converted to the feed basis the unit model bills on by multiplying by recovery) or 'feed'. rated_feed_m3_per_hr and min_feed_m3_per_hr make each skid semicontinuous -- off, or anywhere in [310, 337.67] m3/hr of feed -- which is the plant's scheduling freedom and what makes this a MILP. recovery_min/recovery_max are the membrane train's operating window; they bound the recovery Var, which stays fixed at 'recovery' unless a design or regression pass unfixes it (unfixing makes permeate = recovery * feed bilinear, so the model would classify as MINLP). recuperation_minutes is the restart penalty: for that long after every startup the skid runs at full power but its permeate is off-spec and is diverted to the brine line, so it earns no product. min_uptime_minutes / min_downtime_minutes are the flexops.logic.add_startup_shutdown windows -- how long a skid must stay on after a start and off after a stop. All three are counted in whole time steps, and min_uptime_minutes must be at least recuperation_minutes so that at most one startup can fall inside any recuperation window (a shorter run would burn full power and make nothing but off-spec water anyway).

post_treatment._comment: Remineralization/disinfection on the combined permeate header, downstream of the three RO skids.

product_pump._comment: Delivers post-treated water to the distribution system. The monthly demand is measured at this pump's outlet.

logic._comment: Optional flexops.logic pieces. These are modeling decisions rather than plant properties, so they live here rather than as constants in model.py -- turning any of them off leaves a valid, and different, model. relax_integrality applies flexops.logic.relax to every RO skid, switching its status/startup/shutdown binaries from Binary to UnitInterval: the month becomes an LP that solves in seconds instead of a 26,778-binary MILP. The relaxation is OPTIMISTIC -- a fractional status lets a skid run below its turndown floor and take a fractional startup, so the relaxed cost is a lower bound on the true flexible cost and the reported saving is an UPPER bound on the true saving. Set false to solve the exact MILP (and expect a long run; see solver.options).

solver._comment: prefer is passed to flexcore.solvers.get_solver; if that solver is unavailable or cannot take the problem class, get_solver logs a warning and falls through to its own priority list. options is forwarded verbatim to the Pyomo solver's solve(), so its keys are that solver's own option names -- these are HiGHS's. mip_rel_gap ends the branch and bound once the incumbent is provably within that fraction of optimal, which is what keeps a month of unit commitment tractable; time_limit is the backstop, and a run that hits it is reported rather than silently accepted.

numerics._comment: Post-solve snapping tolerances. A MILP solver returns an idle asset as a few nanowatts either side of zero; a negative one is not merely untidy, since EECO refuses to bill a negative draw. Anything within these of zero is treated as zero.

reporting._comment: Presentation only -- nothing here reaches the model. A month at 15-minute resolution is 2976 points, far too dense to read a 45-minute recuperation window off, so the notebook's single-schedule charts zoom into detail_window instead, and its headline chart averages every day of the horizon onto one time-of-day axis.

scenarios._comment: 'flexible' selects the RO strategy; 'selected' is the case the single-schedule charts render.

tariff._comment: EECO rate_data records. Peak window is 16:00-21:00 (hour_end exclusive), where energy is 4.5x the off-peak price and a monthly demand charge applies. FlexCosting prorates the monthly demand charge onto the horizon.
